Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Insurance Agent
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Vignette:
Arthur remembered the kitchen long after he had left it. It was a Tuesday in November, the kind of evening that turned the house dark before supper. His stepfather had been drinking again, the sharp, sweet tang of cheap whiskey clinging to the curtains and settling in the back of Arthur’s throat. When the arguing started, it quickly turned to the heavy thud of a belt and the cold linoleum against Arthur’s cheek. A siren wailed two streets over, a sound that only made the shouting seem closer. Arthur had wanted the door to open, but it stayed locked. What frightened him most in that moment was the quiet certainty that the man who was supposed to keep him safe had chosen to become the source of it. He felt deeply betrayed by someone he had trusted, and he had come to believe the people responsible would walk away without answer, since they always did. In the years that followed, Arthur’s body never learned to stand down. He kept his ears open during quiet hours, tracking the faint scrape of floorboards or the click of a deadbolt that didn’t belong to him. He reacted to every ordinary noise as though a door were being forced open, his chest tightening even when the house was perfectly still. Memories that did surface arrived without warning, complete with the sour smell of spilled beer and the heat of a raised voice, then vanished as quickly as they had come. Those recollections felt more real and vivid than his own present. He stopped watching television or reading about people who were hurt. Before crossing a threshold, he performed quiet mental rituals, counting backward from seven, certain that if he just held the numbers in place, the past could not follow him forward. He filled every quiet moment with mental arithmetic, reciting policy deductibles and claim codes. These habits sat beside his constant listening, leaving little room for the fragments to surface, though the olfactory recall would occasionally surface when he tried to focus on the claims in front of him. At seventy-one, Arthur still worked as an insurance agent, spending his days at a modest desk downtown, reviewing claims and speaking with clients who walked through the agency doors. The work required him to engage with strangers, and he did so with careful politeness, though every new face at the counter made his shoulders climb toward his ears. He listened for the particular weight of someone’s footsteps behind him, bracing when a courier approached his desk with a package, feeling the same sharp warning in his ribs that had flashed in childhood, even though nothing was actually wrong. His body kept reacting as if he were still crouched in that kitchen, a traitorous system that offered alarms when the air was safe. Over decades, the readiness and the avoidance habits sat side by side, leaving him a solitary figure. He had no family to notice the way he flinched at a dropped stapler, no one to ask why he never turned on the radio, and a home that had grown stricter as his routines thickened. The turning point came on a rain-slicked afternoon when a client’s sudden laugh in the waiting room startled him so violently he knocked his coffee mug to the tile. Standing over the spreading puddle, Arthur realized he could no longer outrun the readiness in his own skin. He had come to see his body as an enemy that refused to acknowledge the years, that kept him locked in a perpetual state of alert long after the original danger had passed. He walked to a community clinic that week, hoping to finally let his nervous system believe he was safe. He feared the mental rituals would stop working, that the fragments would return without warning, but he was willing to sit in a room and talk to a stranger who would not ask for accountability from the past, only help him navigate the present.
